subject: Biology
title: Eusocial Insects: Ant and Bee Colonies
description: A quick, practical guide to Eusocial Insects: Ant and Bee Colonies.

hook.text: In a honeybee colony, 60,000 bees share one mother. Most will never reproduce.

buildup.text: Eusocial insects have a queen who reproduces, workers who labor, and soldiers who defend.

discovery.text: Workers sacrifice their own reproduction to raise sisters who share 75% of their genes.

twist.text: Leafcutter ants farm fungus gardens underground—the only animals besides humans that practice agriculture.

climax.text: A single ant colony can contain millions of individuals acting as a superorganism.

punchline.text: Millions of workers. One queen. Zero debate.

quiz.question: What do leafcutter ants uniquely do?

details.summary: Eusocial insects like ants, bees, and termites live in colonies with reproductive division of labor, cooperative brood care, and overlapping generations. Most individuals are sterile workers that sacrifice reproduction to support the queen's offspring.
details.whyItMatters: Eusociality represents the pinnacle of animal cooperation. Understanding how sterile workers benefit genetically through kin selection reveals fundamental principles about why cooperation evolves in nature.
takeaways: Eusocial colonies have reproductive queens and sterile worker castes
Haplodiploidy in bees makes sisters more related than mother-daughter pairs
Colony-level selection can favor traits harmful to individuals

faq.question: Why do worker bees give up their own reproduction?
faq.answer: Due to haplodiploidy, worker bees share 75 percent of genes with sisters but only 50 percent with their own offspring. Helping the queen produce more sisters can spread a worker's genes more efficiently than reproducing herself.

faq.question: Are ant colonies really like superorganisms?
faq.answer: In many ways, yes. Individual ants cannot survive alone. The colony has specialized castes functioning like organs: soldiers defend, workers forage, and the queen reproduces. The colony as a whole exhibits coordinated behavior no individual controls.
